To recompense someone means to give them something of value to make up for a loss, harm, or effort they experienced because of you or on your behalf.

Think of it this way: imagine a scale. On one side, something happened that was costly to a person — they lost something, suffered something, or gave something up. The scale is now unbalanced. To recompense them is to put something on the other side of the scale to restore the balance and make things fair again.
The Two Main Situations Where You Use It

Recompense covers two closely related situations:

1. Making up for harm or loss
When someone suffers a loss or damage — and you are responsible (or simply in a position to fix it) — you recompense them to make things right. The goal is to restore them, as closely as possible, to the position they were in before the harm happened.

The airline recompensed the passengers for the cancelled flight by refunding their tickets and covering their hotel costs.

The government recompensed the families who lost their homes when the dam burst.

2. Rewarding or paying back someone for their effort, sacrifice, or service
When someone gives their time, energy, or resources for your benefit, recompensing them means acknowledging what they gave and paying them back appropriately.

The general recompensed his soldiers for their years of loyal and dangerous service.

She was never fully recompensed for the hard work she put into building the company from nothing.

This is the most important thing to understand about recompense compared to simpler words like "pay" or "give."

Recompense always carries a moral weight. It implies:

  • That something is genuinely owed
  • That there is a debt — not necessarily in the financial sense, but in the moral sense
  • That the person receiving the recompense has a legitimate claim to it — they are not being given a gift out of generosity alone, but rather being given something that justice demands they receive

When you recompense someone, you are essentially saying: "What happened to you (or what you did) created an obligation, and I am now fulfilling that obligation."

This is why the word feels more serious and formal than just saying "pay" or "reward." There is always an underlying idea of righting a wrong or settling a moral account.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding how recompense sits among similar words will sharpen your understanding considerably.

Reimburse — This is specifically about returning money that someone already spent. If your company pays for a work trip from your own pocket and your employer gives you that money back, they reimburse you. Recompense is broader — the "something of value" given doesn't have to match exactly what was lost; it just has to be sufficient to make things right.

Compensate — Very close to recompense in meaning, and often interchangeable. Compensate, however, tends to feel more clinical, legal, and transactional. Recompense carries a more literary, formal, and morally loaded tone. You'd see "compensate" in a legal contract; you're more likely to see "recompense" in a novel, a speech, or a formal written document.

Reward — Reward leans positive. You reward someone for doing something good. Recompense is more neutral — it applies equally to making up for something bad and acknowledging someone's effort or sacrifice. Also, a reward is often a voluntary extra; recompense is something that is owed.

Repay — Repay is most naturally about returning something specific (usually money or a favour) to its original owner. Recompense is broader and has a stronger moral implication of fairness.

The most natural way to use recompense as a verb is:

Recompense + [person] + for + [the loss/effort/harm]

The company recompensed him for his injuries.
She was recompensed for her years of unpaid work.
Nothing could truly recompense them for what they had endured.

You can also use it without the "for" part when the context already makes the reason clear:

They promised to recompense him, but never did.
The Register: When Do People Use This Word?

Recompense is a formal and somewhat literary word. You won't typically hear it in casual everyday conversation. It appears most naturally in:

  • Formal writing (legal documents, official letters, formal essays)
  • Literature and serious non-fiction
  • Speeches or contexts where elevated language is appropriate
  • Historical or journalistic writing

In everyday speech, people are more likely to say "compensate," "pay back," or "make it up to someone." But if you are reading a novel, a historical text, a legal opinion, or a formal letter and encounter this word, you now know exactly what it means and why it was chosen — the writer wanted to convey not just payment, but the moral weight of a debt being settled.

Here is a simple test to remember the word's essence:

Whenever you see or want to use recompense, ask: "Is something being given back or made right because fairness and justice demand it?" If yes, recompense is the right word. It is never a casual, purely spontaneous gift — it is always an answer to an imbalance that needed to be corrected.
